title: Is the Church Responsible for Antisemitism?
excerpt: From a second-century sermon to a reformer's tract of 1543 to the German churches of the 1930s, Christians taught contempt for the people of Jesus. The New Testament they quoted says something else, and Paul had warned Gentile believers against exactly this.
body:
A student in a history seminar is handed a pamphlet from 1543 that tells German princes to burn synagogues, and she reads the author's name twice, because it is the name on the sign outside the church where she was baptized. A man in his seventies, in church all his life, is sure that hatred of Jews belongs to pagans and tyrants, and that whatever happened in Europe had nothing to do with people like him. A third person was invited to a Good Friday service by a friend and declined because his grandmother had told him what that day once meant for families like theirs in the town she came from.

The skeptic's charge is short. For most of two thousand years, he says, the people who claimed to follow a Jewish teacher taught contempt for his people, and they did it from their pulpits with their Bible open. He wants to know why anyone should take moral instruction from that institution.

The charge has to be granted. The church did not invent every hatred of the Jewish people, and it did not design the death camps. It is responsible for a very great deal, and the record is its own.

## What the Question Asks

The word antisemitism was coined in the nineteenth century for a hatred that claimed to rest on race. Before that there was an older thing, a religious contempt taught by Christians, which historians often call anti-Judaism. Defenders of the church have leaned hard on the difference. The older contempt, they point out, was about belief, so that a Jew who was baptized became, in principle, a brother. The racial hatred of the twentieth century allowed no such door, and its architects despised the church as well.

That distinction is real. It doesn't settle the question, which is about responsibility and not sole authorship. A man who spends years teaching his sons to despise a neighbor has something to answer for when one of them burns the neighbor's house, even if the son went further than the father would have and stopped attending church long before he struck the match.

## What the Church Said and Did

It began with words. In the second century Melito, bishop of Sardis, preached an Easter sermon that survives. It turns at one point to address Israel directly, and it says this: "God has been murdered, the King of Israel has been destroyed by the right hand of Israel." That sentence is the charge later called deicide, the killing of God, and here it is laid on a whole people. Christians were a small and unprotected minority when he said it.

Two centuries on, the church was no longer small. In the 380s John Chrysostom, among the most admired preachers of the Greek-speaking church, gave a series of sermons in Antioch that are still printed under the title *Against the Jews*. His actual targets were members of his own congregation. "Many, I know, respect the Jews and think that their present way of life is a venerable one," he said, and he was alarmed that Christians in Antioch were attending the synagogue's festivals and keeping its fasts. Jews and Christians in that city were on neighborly terms, and their preacher set out to end it. He told his people that the synagogue was "a den of robbers and a lodging for wild beasts," and he said a good deal that was worse.

Augustine, writing in North Africa a generation later, gave the Western church its lasting position, and it cut both ways. Reading a line of the Psalms as a command about the Jewish people, he taught that God had kept them in existence and scattered them so that the church would have them "as witnesses among all nations" to the Scriptures that speak of Christ. They were therefore not to be killed. The [Study Bible](/study/bible) on this site, in its study of Israel and the church, sums up the effect: the teaching "protected Jews in some ways while fixing them in a subordinate place." It was a doctrine of toleration built on contempt, and for long stretches it held.

It didn't hold when it mattered most. In 1096 the armies gathering for the First Crusade turned on the Jewish communities of the Rhineland before they ever left for the East, and killed them at Worms and Mainz while local bishops tried to shelter them and failed. In 1144, at Norwich in England, the lie began that Jews murdered Christian children for their blood, and that slander set off massacres for centuries. In 1215 the same council that required every Christian to confess once a year ordered Jews to wear clothing that marked them out. England expelled its Jews in 1290, France did so more than once, and Spain followed in 1492. Holy Week became dangerous. The notes in this site's Study Bible record that Good Friday preaching and passion plays were occasions for violence against Jewish neighbors in medieval and early modern Europe.

The Reformation did not break the pattern. In 1523 Martin Luther wrote a tract called *That Jesus Christ Was Born a Jew*, in the hope that Jews would now hear the gospel and believe it. Twenty years later, when the conversions he had hoped for had not come, he wrote *On the Jews and Their Lies*. It advised the rulers of Germany to set fire to synagogues and schools, to tear down Jewish homes, to confiscate prayer books, to forbid rabbis to teach, and to drive the people out if all else failed.

## The Third Reich

Four centuries later it was put to use. The men who built the racial state in Germany were not Christians in any sense the creeds would recognize. They also knew what was in the church's cupboard. The Study Bible's note on John 8 records that the verse Luther had turned against the Jews in 1543 was used again in Nazi propaganda, including in books for children.

The German churches did worse than fail to resist. The history course on this site tells it in its chapter on [the church in the twentieth century](/theology/history/the-global-church). The regime that came to power in 1933 had the welcome of most of Germany's Protestants. One movement inside the church, which named itself the German Christians, wanted church and state fused, and it took the state's racial rule into the church, which meant that a minister could lose his pulpit for having Jewish ancestry. A minority of pastors refused and issued the Barmen Declaration in 1934. It was brave, and the course is candid about its limit. Barmen, it says, "said nothing directly about the persecution of the Jews, and most of its signers never did either."

There were Christians who sheltered Jews at the risk of their own lives, and their names should be honored. They were exceptions. In October of 1945 the surviving leaders of the German Protestant churches confessed in a public declaration at Stuttgart that they had not witnessed with enough courage or prayed, believed and loved as they should have. The course's comment on that confession is hard to improve: "it came too late for six million people."

So the distinction between religious contempt and racial hatred has to bear this much weight and no more. The church did not teach the theory of race, and its doctrine never called for extermination. But for fifteen hundred years we had taught Europe that the Jews were a people under a curse, and we had made them strangers by law, by dress and by sermon. When a regime arrived that wanted them dead, it found a population already trained to look away. We prepared the ground.

## Is the Hatred in the New Testament?

Some scholars, Jewish and Christian, have pressed the charge further back. They argue that the contempt was not a later corruption, and that it grows from the New Testament's own sentences. Three places carry most of the argument.

The first is the cry of the crowd before Pilate: "His blood be on us and on our children!" (Matthew 27:25). For more than a thousand years Christians read that as a self-imposed curse resting on every Jew ever born. The second is the Gospel of John, which uses the phrase "the Jews" some seventy times, often for the opponents of Jesus, and in which Jesus tells a group of them, "You are of your father the devil" (John 8:44). The third is Paul's angry sentence about those in Judea "who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets" (1 Thessalonians 2:15).

The charge has to be granted this much: these sentences were the ones used. No account of what they first meant undoes what was done with them. The Study Bible's note on John 8 says it without flinching: "Jewish readers do not need to be persuaded that this verse has been dangerous."

But what a text was used for and what it says are different questions, and here the difference is very large.

Every one of these sentences was written by a Jew, about an argument among Jews. Matthew's crowd is a particular crowd on a particular morning, and Matthew himself says who worked it up: "the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd" (Matthew 27:20). A crowd in a courtyard cannot bind a nation, and the law of Moses forbids punishing children for what their fathers did (Deuteronomy 24:16). Matthew has also already told his readers what this blood is for. At the supper the night before, Jesus calls it "my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matthew 26:28). If that blood is on anyone's children, it is on them for pardon.

John's usage is odder than the slogan allows. In his Gospel the parents of a blind man are afraid to speak "because they feared the Jews" (John 9:22), and the parents are Jews. The disciples lock their doors "for fear of the Jews" (John 20:19), and every one of them is a Jew. The phrase in those places plainly means the authorities in Jerusalem, as the Study Bible's notes on John explain, and not a people. The same Gospel has Jesus say to a Samaritan woman, "salvation is from the Jews" (John 4:22).

As for the harshness, the prophets were harsher. Isaiah opens with "Ah, sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, offspring of evildoers" (Isaiah 1:4), and no one has ever called Isaiah a hater of Israel. This was how Israel's own preachers spoke to Israel, from inside.

And that is exactly where the misreading happened. Words spoken by Jews to Jews, inside a family quarrel, were picked up within a few generations by Gentiles who were outside the family. Once the readers were no longer kin, the same sentences did different work. A prophet's rebuke from within became, in another people's mouth, an accusation from above. When those Gentiles gained the power of the state, the accusation acquired teeth. The New Testament did not change. Its readers did, and we were the readers.

## Who Killed Jesus

The charge of deicide deserves its own answer, because the New Testament gives one and it is not the one Melito gave.

The first Christians prayed about the crucifixion in these words: "there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel" (Acts 4:27). Everyone is in that sentence. The sentence of death was Roman and so was the cross, and the creed that Christians recite names only one man in connection with his death: he suffered "under Pontius Pilate." Peter, preaching in Jerusalem, tells his hearers that they "acted in ignorance" (Acts 3:17). Jesus, dying, asks pardon for the men doing it: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34). And he had already said who was finally responsible for his death. "No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord" (John 10:18).

Christian teaching at its most careful has said that the answer to the question is in the first person plural. He died for our sins. A church that needed someone else to blame for the cross had stopped believing its own gospel about it.

## What Paul Told the Gentiles

There is one passage in the New Testament written directly to Gentile Christians about how to regard the Jewish people, and the church managed for centuries to read around it.

Paul opens it with grief. He has "great sorrow and unceasing anguish" (Romans 9:2) for his own people, and he lists what is theirs: "the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises" (Romans 9:4). He adds that "from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ" (Romans 9:5). Then he asks the question the later church would answer wrongly. "I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means!" (Romans 11:1).

His picture is an olive tree. Some natural branches have been broken off, and Gentile believers, a wild shoot, have been grafted in among the rest. The very next thing he says is a warning to the shoot. "Do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you" (Romans 11:18). And again: "So do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20). He ends by saying that the people who have not believed are still "beloved for the sake of their forefathers. For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" (Romans 11:28-29).

Christians read the details of these chapters differently. The Study Bible's note on [Romans 11](/study/bible/romans/11) sets out the main readings of "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26) and does not force a choice, and this essay adds nothing to what Paul says there about anyone's standing before God. What no reading can get around is the instruction. The one attitude Paul forbids Gentile Christians to take toward the Jewish people is arrogance, and it is the attitude the church then took for the better part of two millennia.

It should also have been impossible to forget whose faith this was. Matthew's first line calls Jesus "the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). He was circumcised on the eighth day. He went to the synagogue on the Sabbath, "as was his custom" (Luke 4:16). His mother, his twelve apostles and nearly every author of the New Testament were Jews. Decades after the resurrection the leaders in Jerusalem could tell Paul, "You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed" (Acts 21:20). The great dispute of the first church was whether Gentiles could be let in at all. Within a few lifetimes the guests were treating the household as intruders.

## The Repentance, and What It Has Not Done

After 1945 the churches began to say so. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council declared that what happened in the passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today," and that "the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures." It said that the church "decries hatred, persecutions, displays of anti-Semitism, directed against Jews at any time and by anyone." In 1994 a large Lutheran body in America formally repudiated Luther's writings against the Jews. The page on this site about [Judaism, Islam and Jesus](/questions/religions/judaism-islam-and-jesus) records other such statements and says for itself that the old reading of Matthew 27:25 is false.

These statements were right, and it's fair to notice how they came about. The church did not find its way back to Romans 11 by reading. It was driven there by a catastrophe, after the people it had wronged for centuries had been murdered by the million. A repentance that needed that much evidence shouldn't be offered as proof of the church's moral insight.

A statement also does little on its own. The passion story is still read aloud every spring in churches whose members have never been told how it was once used. Sermons still make "the Pharisees" a lazy word for everything false in religion, as though Paul had not been one. Christians still disagree, seriously and in good faith, about how to state the relation between the church and Israel, and that discussion is not finished. What can be asked of every pulpit is simpler, and one of the Study Bible's notes on John puts it in a single line: "teach them in a way no Jewish neighbor would have reason to fear."

The man who has been in church all his life was right that hatred of Jews is a pagan thing. It is foreign to the gospel in every line. He was wrong about who had carried it. It was preached by bishops and printed by reformers. It was preached in Holy Week by people who held the same creed he holds, and they were not monsters. They were sure of their Bible, and nobody had made them look at what that sureness cost the family down the street.

Over the cross the governor had a notice fixed, and John records its wording: "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews" (John 19:19). The priests asked him to change it and he refused. Crucifixes all over Europe carried that notice, often cut down to its initials, above congregations that had been taught to despise his people. It hung in front of us for centuries, and we did not read it.

*"Do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you."* (Romans 11:18)

*"For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable."* (Romans 11:29)
